note.explanation: To measure length accurately, choose an instrument with a suitable least count, line it up correctly with the object, and read the scale with your eye directly above it. For smaller objects, Vernier Callipers and a micrometer screw gauge give more precise readings than a metre rule.
examples: For the Vernier Callipers example: 4.3 cm + (0.01 cm × 4) = 4.34 cm.
For the screw gauge example: 6.5 mm + (25 × 0.01 mm) = 6.75 mm.
note.checkAnswer: The least count is the smallest measurement that can be taken accurately with an instrument.
note.simple: Least count tells you the smallest length an instrument can measure accurately. Keep your eye straight above the scale so the reading does not look different.
note.checkQuestion: What is the least count of the Vernier Callipers described in this section?
note.title: Measuring length accurately
steps: Choose the instrument that suits the size of the object.
Place the object correctly and make sure the scale starts from the object's edge.
Read the scale with your eye directly above it to avoid parallax error.
For Vernier Callipers or a screw gauge, combine the main scale reading with the smaller scale reading multiplied by the least count.
Check for zero error and correct the observed reading as required.

mcqs.stem: A Vernier Callipers has 1 mm main-scale divisions and 10 Vernier divisions equal to 9 mm. What is its least count?
rationales: Correct: one Vernier division is 0.9 mm, so the difference is 1.0 mm − 0.9 mm = 0.1 mm.
This is the main-scale division, not the difference between one main-scale and one Vernier-scale division.
This is the least count of the screw gauge in the section, not this Vernier Callipers.
This is the size of one Vernier division, not the least count.

options: The eye is not directly above the scale.
The instrument has a small least count.
The object is placed against the zero mark.
The instrument is made of metal.
mcqs.stem: What causes parallax error when reading a metre rule?
rationales: Correct: viewing from an angle makes the object appear to have a different length.
A small least count improves the measurement and does not cause parallax error.
Starting at the zero mark is the normal method and does not by itself cause parallax error.
The material of the instrument is not the cause of parallax error.

options: The difference between one main-scale division and one Vernier-scale division
The length of the whole Vernier scale
The total number of main-scale divisions
The distance between the two jaws
mcqs.stem: How is the least count of the Vernier Callipers defined in this section?
rationales: Correct: the least count is the difference between one main-scale division and one Vernier-scale division.
The whole scale length is not the definition of least count.
Counting main-scale divisions does not determine the least count by itself.
The jaw distance changes with the object and is not the instrument's least count.

mcqs.stem: Which part of Vernier Callipers is used to measure the depth of a hollow object?
rationales: The outside jaws measure external dimensions of an object.
The inside jaws measure internal dimensions of an object.
Correct: the projecting tail or depth gauge is used to measure depth.
A circular scale is part of the screw gauge, not the depth-measuring part of Vernier Callipers.

mcqs.stem: A screw gauge has a pitch of 0.5 mm and 50 divisions on its circular scale. What is its least count?
rationales: Correct: least count = pitch ÷ divisions = 0.5 mm ÷ 50 = 0.01 mm.
This is ten times the calculated least count.
This is not the pitch divided by the number of circular-scale divisions.
This is the pitch, not the least count.

options: Subtract the zero error from the observed measurement.
Add the zero error to the observed measurement.
Multiply the observed measurement by the zero error.
mcqs.stem: A Vernier Callipers has its Vernier zero to the right of the main-scale zero when its jaws are closed. How should its zero error be corrected?
rationales: Correct: the instrument reads slightly more than the actual length, so subtract the zero error.
Adding it would make the reading still larger and less accurate.
The section gives correction by addition or subtraction, not multiplication.
Ignoring a zero error leaves the observed measurement uncorrected.

options: Read the sleeve just before the thimble, then add circular-scale reading × least count.
Multiply the sleeve reading by the circular-scale reading.
Subtract the sleeve reading from the circular-scale reading.
mcqs.stem: Which method is used to find a screw-gauge measurement?
rationales: Correct: the reading is the main-scale reading plus circular-scale reading multiplied by the least count.
The two readings are not multiplied together.
The section does not calculate the measurement by subtracting these readings.
The main-scale reading must also be included.

mcqs.stem: What least count is given for the micrometer screw gauge in this section?
rationales: This is the least count of the Vernier Callipers described in the section.
This is the least count of the metre rule and measuring tape in the section.
Correct: the screw gauge's least count is 0.01 mm.
This is the screw gauge pitch in the described example, not its least count.

written.text: Suppose, an object is placed between the two jaws, the position of the Vernier scale on the main scale is shown in Fig. 1.3. Read the main scale marking just infront of zero of the Vernier scale. It shows 4.3 cm. Find the length of object.

rubric.why: The main-scale reading is needed as the starting part of the measurement.
rubric.how: Read the main scale just in front of zero of the Vernier scale.

rubric.why: The Vernier contribution depends on using the correct least count.
rubric.description: Use the Vernier least count of 0.01 cm.
rubric.how: Use the least count stated in the worked example.

rubric.why: The aligned Vernier division gives the extra part of the measurement.
rubric.description: Use Vernier-scale reading 4 multiplied by the least count.
rubric.how: Add 0.01 × 4 to the main-scale reading.

rubric.why: The final measurement must include both scale readings.
rubric.how: State the sum with the correct unit.

modelAnswer: Main scale reading = 4.3 cm
Vernier scale reading = 4
Length of object = Main scale reading + (Least count × Vernier scale reading)

written.text: Suppose when a steel sheet is placed in between the anvil and spindle, the position of circular scale is shown in Fig.1.7. Read the marking on the sleeve just before the thimble. It shows 6.5 mm. Read the circular scale marking which is in line with the main scale. This shows 25. Find the thickness.

rubric.why: The sleeve reading is the main-scale contribution to the thickness.
rubric.how: Read the sleeve marking just before the thimble.

rubric.why: The circular-scale reading supplies the smaller measured part.
rubric.how: Use the circular-scale marking in line with the main scale.

rubric.why: The circular-scale reading must be multiplied by the least count.
rubric.description: Apply the least count of 0.01 mm.
rubric.how: Calculate 25 × 0.01 mm and add it to 6.5 mm.

rubric.how: State the calculated thickness in millimetres.

modelAnswer: Main scale reading = 6.5 mm

written.text: Q1.9. (a) For what purpose, a Vernier Callipers is used? (b) Name its two main parts. (c) How is least count found? (d) What is meant by zero error?
written.finalAnswer: It measures small lengths; its two scales are the main scale and Vernier scale; least count is the difference between one main-scale division and one Vernier-scale division; zero error occurs when the scale zeros do not coincide with the jaws joined.

rubric.why: The instrument's purpose identifies when it should be selected.
rubric.description: State a suitable use of Vernier Callipers.
rubric.how: Say that it measures small lengths, thickness, diameter, width or depth.

rubric.why: The two scales are the instrument's main measuring parts.
rubric.how: Write main scale and Vernier scale.

rubric.why: The definition of least count is a key measurement principle.
rubric.description: Define how least count is found.
rubric.how: Give the difference between one main-scale division and one Vernier-scale division.

rubric.why: Recognising zero error is necessary to correct an observed reading.
rubric.how: State that it occurs when the zeros fail to coincide when the jaws are joined.

modelAnswer: (a) A Vernier Callipers is used to measure small lengths down to 1/10th of a millimetre. It can measure the thickness, diameter, width or depth of an object.
(b) Its two scales are the main scale and Vernier (sliding) scale.
(c) Least count = 1 M.S div − 1 V.S div.
(d) If the zeros of the main scale and Vernier scale do not exactly coincide when the jaws are joined, there is an error in the instrument called zero error.

written.text: Q1.11. Which reading out of A, B and C shows the correct length and why?
written.finalAnswer: B, because the eye is directly above the ruler and avoids parallax error.

rubric.why: The correct viewing position gives the correct length.
rubric.how: Select B.

modelAnswer: Reading B is correct.
The eye is directly above the ruler at B, so the reading is not affected by parallax error.

written.text: Q1.3. The minimum main scale reading of a micrometer screw gauge is 1 mm and there are 100 divisions on the circular scale. When thimble is rotated once, 1 mm is its measurement on the main scale. What is the least count of the instrument?

rubric.why: The least count formula requires pitch divided by circular-scale divisions.
rubric.description: Use the correct formula and values.
rubric.how: Calculate 1 mm divided by 100.

rubric.why: The final least count gives the smallest accurate measurement.
rubric.how: Write the answer in millimetres.

modelAnswer: Pitch of the screw gauge = 1 mm
Least count = Pitch of the screw gauge / No. of divisions on the circular scale

written.text: Q1.4. You are provided a metre scale and a bundle of pencils; how can the diameter of a pencil be measured using the metre scale with the same precision as that of Vernier Callipers? Describe briefly.
written.finalAnswer: Place 10 pencils side by side, measure their total width with the metre scale, and divide by 10 to find the diameter of one pencil.

rubric.why: Measuring several pencils together makes the total width easier to measure accurately.
rubric.how: Place 10 pencils side by side, close together.

rubric.why: A total measurement is needed before finding the width of one pencil.
rubric.how: Use the metre scale to measure the total width.

rubric.why: Dividing the total width gives the average diameter of one pencil.
rubric.description: Divide by the number of pencils.
rubric.how: Divide the measured total by 10.

rubric.why: The result must answer the question about a single pencil.
rubric.how: State that the quotient is the diameter of one pencil.

modelAnswer: Place 10 pencils side by side, with their lengths parallel and the pencils touching.
Measure the total width of the 10 pencils using the metre scale.
Divide the total width by 10.
The result is the diameter of one pencil.

written.text: Q1.5. The end of a metre scale is worn out. Where will you place a pencil to find the length?
written.finalAnswer: Place one end of the pencil at a clear mark such as 1 cm, then subtract that starting reading from the reading at the other end.

rubric.why: A worn zero edge cannot be used as a reliable starting point.
rubric.description: Use a clear scale mark instead of the worn end.
rubric.how: Place the pencil at a visible mark such as 1 cm.

rubric.why: The difference between the two readings gives the pencil's length.
rubric.description: Find the length from the two readings.
rubric.how: Subtract the starting reading from the final reading.

modelAnswer: Place one end of the pencil at a clear mark on the scale, such as 1 cm.
Read the mark at the other end of the pencil.
Subtract the starting reading from the reading at the other end to find the length.

written.text: Q1.6. Why is it better to place the object close to the metre scale?
written.finalAnswer: It reduces parallax error because the object is close to the scale while it is being read.

rubric.why: Parallax error is a common source of incorrect length readings.
rubric.how: Mention parallax error.

rubric.how: State that this helps reduce or avoid the reading error.

modelAnswer: It is better to place the object close to the metre scale to reduce parallax error when taking the measurement.

written.finalAnswer: (i) Vernier Callipers, using the inside jaws. (ii) Vernier Callipers, using the tail or depth gauge.

written.text: Q1.3. State the similarities and differences between Vernier Callipers and micrometer screw gauge.
written.finalAnswer: Both measure small lengths and have a main scale and a second scale. Vernier Callipers uses a Vernier scale and has a least count of 0.1 mm; a micrometer screw gauge uses a circular scale and has a least count of 0.01 mm.

rubric.why: A valid similarity states what both instruments are used for.
rubric.how: State that both measure small lengths.

rubric.why: Both instruments use scale readings to measure length.
rubric.how: Mention that each has a main scale and another measuring scale.

rubric.how: Vernier Callipers has a Vernier scale; the screw gauge has a circular scale.

rubric.why: The least counts show the different precision of the instruments.

modelAnswer: Both instruments are used to measure small lengths and each has a main scale and another scale.
Vernier Callipers has a Vernier (sliding) scale; a micrometer screw gauge has a circular scale on the thimble.
The least count of Vernier Callipers is 0.1 mm.
The least count of a micrometer screw gauge is 0.01 mm.

explain.title: Least count
explain.body: Least count is the smallest measurement that can be taken accurately with an instrument. The metre rule's least count is 1 mm. In this section, Vernier Callipers has a least count of 0.1 mm and a micrometer screw gauge has a least count of 0.01 mm.

explain.title: Read the ruler from above
explain.body: Parallax error is due to incorrect position of eye when taking measurements. It can be avoided by keeping eye perpendicular to the scale reading. In Fig. 1.1, point B gives the correct reading.

explain.title: Vernier Callipers
explain.body: It is an instrument used to measure small lengths down to 1/10th of a millimetre. It can be used to measure the thickness, diameter, width or depth of an object. The two scales on it are: (a) A main scale which has marking of 1mm each. (b) A Vernier (sliding) scale of length 9 mm and it is divided into 10 equal parts.

explain.title: Zero error
explain.body: If the zeros of the main scale and Vernier scale do not exactly coincide when the jaws are joined, the instrument has zero error. A Vernier zero to the right of the main-scale zero reads slightly more, so subtract the zero error. A Vernier zero to the left reads slightly less, so add the zero error.

explain.title: Micrometer screw gauge
explain.body: A screw gauge measures very small lengths such as the diameter of a wire or the thickness of a metal sheet. Its least count is the pitch divided by the number of divisions on the circular scale.

mistakes: Reading a ruler from an angle instead of keeping the eye directly above the scale causes parallax error.
Forgetting to multiply the smaller-scale reading by the least count loses marks.
Adding the Vernier or circular-scale contribution incorrectly, instead of adding it to the main-scale reading, gives the wrong measurement.
Using the wrong correction direction for zero error: subtract for a Vernier zero to the right and add for a Vernier zero to the left.
Leaving out units or writing a reading with more precision than the instrument supports.
